a bunch of stuff and then automatically
being able to do it. You got it in a
completely different way. I guarantee
somewhere in your life, whether you know
how to play a musical instrument, you're
really good at your job, or just
learning how to walk, you've gone
through this process intuitively, but
you've never actually thought through it
and tried to apply it to writing. And
so, this is what we're going to do.
We're going to take all of the research
around humans learning complex skills,
and we're going to look at how we might
actually apply it to writing to fix this
broken culture about how writers are
actually made. So, this research goes
all the way back to 1993. It started
with K. Anders Ericsson and some of his
colleagues. They studied world-class
violinists, chess grandmasters,
athletes, and others. And what they
found is the people at the top weren't
born there. Again, there is no such
thing as natural talent that will make
you great. They practiced, but they
practiced differently. They did
something called deliberate practice.
This is what Anders Ericsson named it,
he called it deliberate practice. And
deliberate practice, when done right,
doesn't help you survive a wicked
environment, it completely dismantles a
wicked environment and rebuilds it as a
kind one. And there are five conditions
that go into every kind environment. So
again, there are some things like
playing the guitar where the kind
environment is kind of natural, but with
a wicked environment like the writing
environment, you have to on purpose
dismantle the wicked environment and
build it back up as a kind environment.
Once you've done that, then building
skill becomes very straightforward and
very natural, just like other skills.
And there's five conditions that have to
go in place. So, let's walk through each
of these. And again, this isn't all the
finding. I'm going to put down all the
different links to the research in the
notes of this video, so you can go read
it yourself if you don't believe me. So,
there's five conditions that go into
this. Condition number one is you have
to practice specific skills. So, writing
is not one skill. It's actually lots of
different skills all kind of shoved
together under this umbrella of writing.
Again, let's go back to playing the
guitar. Playing the guitar is not
actually one skill. It's lots of
different skills. It's finger placement.
It's chords. It's learning to play under
different tempos and different rhythms.
It's learning how to string the guitar.
How to tune the guitar. How to strum the
guitar. How to pick the guitar. There
are actually dozens and dozens of skills
that live under this umbrella of playing
the guitar. Writing's the same way. It's
learning how to write dialogue, learning
how to write action, learning how to
write exposition, show versus tell,
point of view, setting, pacing,
narrative drive, grammar, the five
commandments of storytelling, so many
things that I've talked about on this
channel. All of these individual skills
that come together under this writing
thing. So, if you want to learn writing,
you can't learn it by trying to do all
of the things at the same time. Again,
coming back to playing the guitar. I
don't sit down and try to play really
complicated music if I'm just learning
how to play the guitar. I learn the
easiest chord first, the second easiest.
I learn like three chords and I just try
to do those over and over and over until
I can do them without thinking and then
I start building from there. So, you
have to practice specific skills until
they become natural and then you can and
building up from there. This is why I
just right your novel is like telling a
new pianist to learn everything at once
by performing a Beethoven song live. You
cannot learn to write a great novel by
trying to write a great novel. It
doesn't make any sense. If you look at
the actual research, this is the
opposite that you should be doing. The
last thing you do is take all the
individual skills you practiced and
figured out how to do them together and
then try to write a novel. This is the
thing. It repairs pattern repetition
because you're drilling repeatedly these
individual skills until you can do them
without thinking. Let's just look at
show versus tell. Almost every writer I
work with does not know how to show and
does not know when to show versus when
to tell. We have to drill it over and
over and over. They have to fail over
and over and over until they get just
that one skill right and then we can
move on to other skills. This is how it
works. Think about how you've learned
anything. You started with the simple
thing. You kept practicing until you can
do it really well and then you moved on
to other things. So that's condition
number one. You have to practice
specific skills. Condition number two is
you have to diagnose against a standard.
Remember that anytime you were getting
feedback that was unclear or wrong or
subjective, it wasn't helping you get
better. It was actually making you
worse. So let's imagine that you needed
to go get an MRI at the hospital. Get an
MRI scan. So last year I had a knee
injury doing Brazilian Jiu Jitsu and I
had to go in and get an MRI of my knee.
So let's imagine I came out of that and
the tech looked at my scan and was kind
of like, "Hey, you know, what do you
think all of these colors mean? I'm not
really sure." I would be running out of
that hospital because you don't want
somebody that doesn't know the standard
diagnosing what's going on. A real
diagnosis measures against a defined
standard, not how the scan feels to
somebody. Writing groups, AI, beta
readers, your mom, or your sister
reading your stuff, they have no
standard. There is no standard they're
judging against other than how they feel
internally, which is completely
subjective. So, first, you have to have
a standard of what you're trying to
practice against, and this fixes the
whole rule stability or feedback
accuracy inside of the Wicked
environment by actually diagnosing
against a standard. So, number one was
you have to break it down into
individual skills and practice those.
Number two is diagnose against a
standard, and number three is you have
to have expert analysis. So, let's go
back to that MRI thing. Let's say the
tech came in with the results of my MRI,
and they told you like, "You know what?
I'm actually really busy. I'm going to
go over to the patient in the next room.
I'm going to just hand them your scan,
and I'm going to have them tell you
whether or not you need surgery or not.
They're pretty smart. They can figure it
out." Again, you would run out of that
hospital as fast as possible. And yet,
constantly, writers hand their writing
to a group of fellow amateurs and just
ask for their opinion. An expert has
seen a thousand versions of your scene.
This is a thing. I don't want an MRI
tech that needs to ask somebody else. I
want the MRI tech that's been through
school, that's gotten their degree,
that's looked at thousands of scans and
been able to judge them against the
standard, and they have been correct.
That's what you need. You need expert
feedback. You need that above all else.
You need somebody that can look at your
writing and figure out, "Here's what's
wrong. Here's what's right. Here's how
to fix what's wrong." and tell you in
concrete specific details. That's what
you need, expert analysis. This is how
you get past this thing of never knowing
if you're doing it right or not. So,
again, this is what the research says is
that the third thing you need is expert
analysis. Let's get to the fourth thing,
because once you are breaking things up
into individual skills, once you're
diagnosing to a standard, once you have
an expert doing it, what is the fourth
thing that actually like pulls all this
together and makes the biggest
difference? A short feedback loop. Every
field study, whether it's musicians,
surgeons, chess players, any field
that's applied any of this research to
it, this is the thing that matters. How
close is you practicing and getting the
feedback? How close in time? So again,
if I'm playing the guitar and I play the
wrong note, I immediately know I played
it wrong. Or if I'm playing something
with a teacher and they see me do
something wrong and they immediately
stop me and tell me how I need to do it
right. That shortening the feedback loop
is one of the most important things you
can do. And yet, what do we do in
writing? The feedback loop is usually
months or years. You sit alone writing a
100,000-word manuscript and then you
hand it off to an editor hoping they can
address what's wrong. But again, if you
go too long between practicing and
getting feedback, you've made so many
mistakes in there that you can't hope to
fix them all. You can't learn how to get
better. The only way you learn how to
get better is by practicing a small
individual piece, getting feedback and
doing that over and over until you can
do it right and then moving on to the
next thing. You have to solve the
feedback speed. This is what we see over
and over and over. What's the fifth
thing? It's a clear roadmap of growth.
No guitarist sits down and tries to
learn the most complex things at first.
They start with the basic chords and
then build up from there. Same thing
with the woodworker. A brand new
woodworker who doesn't know how to do
anything doesn't try to build a rocking
chair. They just try to build a simple
box. They start with a small unit, get
good at that, and build up from there.
And yet, what do we tell writers to do?
Sit down and write your novel. Take that
epic fantasy trilogy you've had in your
head since you were a kid and just sit
down and give it a go. And that is the
exact same thing as telling a woodworker
that's never done anything to just build
a rocking chair or telling somebody that
wants to learn how to dance to pick the
most complicated choreography and just
give it a go. It doesn't make any sense.
There has to be a clear roadmap. And
inside of writing, it's right there
staring at us in the face. Think about
how a reader actually takes in a book.
They don't experience a novel as a
novel. They don't even experience it as
a series of like arcs in the story, a
series of acts. They don't even
experience it one scene at a time. They
experience it one sentence at a time.
They read a sentence, then the next one,
then the next one. And we've all read
those books where after a few sentences,
we realize this book is not very good
and we move on. And so, if you want to
learn how to write a novel, you start at
the sentence level. You break it down.
And at the sentence level, you've got to
learn all the very specific things. What
does a good sentence of dialogue look
like and how do you write it? What does
a good sentence of showing versus
telling look like and how do you write
it? Same thing with point of view, same
thing with setting description,
exposition, all of these things. This is
how you learn. It's the five conditions
that go into it. You have to break down
the complex skill into individual
skills. You have to practice those
individually against an actual standard,
have an expert judge whether or not
you're hitting the standard and give you
very fast feedback. So, you're
practicing a few sentences at a time and
then getting feedback and then you're
building up the skills in a natural
order that you need to learn them. Those
are the five conditions that show up in
the research. And think about this, in
the typical way we are told to learn how
to write, every one of those items don't
exist. The wickedness of writing is
because we don't take the research
that's sitting there right in front of
us since 1993, extract the lessons and
apply them to writing. We are taking the
word of these writers that wrote this
stuff down that doesn't make any sense,
and we keep just trying to do it. And
this is why, of all the creative fields,
us as writers are so far behind, and
we're telling people, "Maybe you're just
a bad writer, and you can't be helped."
Or maybe you just need to try it for
another 10 years, and maybe one day it
will click. It is time to move on from
this old way of doing things, apply the
research in the science that we know
works in other fields, and apply it to
the writing world. So, let's go back to
2015 when I started working with Sean. I
was trying to learn how to write, and it
just wasn't working. And so, eventually
he said, "You know what? You're not
allowed to work on novels anymore.
You're not even allowed to work on short
stories. Even a scene is too long for
you." And what he told me is, "Tim, I
hate to tell you, but you can't even
write a sentence." And so, that is what
we started working on is just how do you
write one great sentence that will get
the reader to read the next one and the
next one and the next one. And I'll tell
you, it bruised my ego. I did not like
it. I was mad at him. I thought it was
ridiculous. I've been trying to write
for over 10 years. Who are you to tell
me? And yet, I thought, "Well, I do have
this world-class editor with like this
huge track record in the publishing
industry trying to help me. Maybe I
should give it a try." And after a few
weeks, I started noticing something. My
sentences were getting better. And then
after a couple months, I noticed, "Man,
my sentences are getting really strong."
And then he let me move on and write a
scene. And then I wrote scenes that for
the first time actually worked. I could
go back and look at my old writing and
see where everything is broken. What I
couldn't see before, I could see now,
and I could start writing stuff that
worked. And then fast forward, I wrote
my book, The and it works.
It's a great book. People love it.
Again, sold thousands of copies,
hundreds of reviews, really good
feedback, and I can consistently write
working writing now because I slowed
down, applied the research of deliberate
practice, and learned the actual skills
of writing. Just like if I want to learn
to play the guitar, I got to learn the
chords, I got to learn how to strum, I
got to learn how to tune my guitar, I
got to learn all these things, and then
I can go off and play something
beautiful, something I'm proud of. But I
had to slow down and learn the skills.
None of this is magic, and that's the
point. This is not magic, this is not
talent, this is not the muse. Magic is
what the writing world has been selling
all along. Slog away and hope that the
muse blesses you, hope that you're not
one of those bad writers that's
hopeless. Instead, let's just look at
how humans acquire skill and apply that
to writing. And lo and behold, writers
actually noticeably get better at the
craft to the point that they can write
publishable work on a repeated basis.
So, if you've been working on your

## The Writing Doom Loop (and How to Beat It)

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n4TMG4WhQO0>
Caption file: n4TMG4WhQO0.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Writing Mindset & Productivity
Secondary Topics: Writer Development, Editing & Revision, Author Career & Business, Reader Experience & Engagement
Tertiary Topics: Motivation & Desire, Revision, Beats, Audience, Description, Scene Structure, Character Arc, Feedback

In 2013, I hit a wall with my writing
and I decided to quit. I had this
manuscript I'd been working on for 2
years. I wrote an entire draft and I
revised it, then I revised it again,
then revised it again, and it still was
a complete mess and nowhere near
publishable. And this was after like a
decade of trying to do this on my own.
Writing books, realizing they're not
good enough, getting halfway through,
giving up, and on this just write revise
loop. And so finally, I threw up my
hands and decided to quit. And I want to
know if this is something that you can
relate to. So think about this. Maybe
you write a draft of something. It could
be a few chapters, it could be half a
book, an entire manuscript, and then you
put it in a drawer like you're supposed
to and leave it alone for a couple weeks
and you come back and read it and you
realize something's wrong. It's not
working. And so you decide, okay, I need
to go learn more about writing. So you
go read a book, maybe take an online
course, maybe watch a masterclass by
some famous writer. You learn a bunch of
stuff and you realize like okay, now
I've got all this I'm going to go back
and I'm going to revise that novel. So
then you do that, then you put it in a
drawer, then you read it, realize you
made some things a little bit better,
other things maybe got worse. You're not
really sure. And so you have to go learn
some more. So back to reading and
courses and then you try to revise it
and round and round you go trying to
write and revise this novel over and
over and over. So does that something
that you can relate to? This is what I
call the writer zoom loop. This endless
write and revise loop we get stuck in
trying to write a novel that actually
works, that's actually publishable. And
if you're nodding along right now, you
know exactly what I'm talking about.
Most writers spend years in this loop. I
spent over a decade in it and by 2013,
I'd had enough. So I decided to stop. I
give up on writing. I must just not have
the talent or the writing gene or
whatever it is. So it's just time to cut
my losses and move on. So I left that
manuscript in the folder on my desktop
with the other dozen half-done
manuscripts in various states of
unfinished, and I decided I'm going to
move on with my life and find something
else to do with my time. So, what was
actually going wrong here? Because I was
following all of the conventional
advice. I was working on my book,
writing every day. I read the craft
books, I joined writers groups, I went
through online courses. And when I
finished the draft, I'd start the
rewrites because, you know, Ernest
Hemingway said that the only kind of
writing is rewriting. And he said, "The
first draft of everything is shit." And
so, you have to revise. And then Robert
Graves said, "There's no such thing as

hand-in-hand with what Anne Lamott says
in Bird by Bird when she says, "The only
way I can get anything written at all is
to write really, really shitty first
drafts." So, I was doing exactly what
every famous writer said to do, all the
courses said to do, and yet it wasn't
working. I wasn't getting any closer to
to writing a draft of a novel I was
actually proud to publish that readers
would love. And here's something nobody
ever seems to talk about. Now, at this
point, I have been in the publishing
industry for 18 years. I've worked with
brand new writers, debut writers, all
the way through career writers that have
been doing it for a really long time.
I've seen behind the scenes, I know lots
of agents, lots of editors. I've just
been around the industry. And this is
one of those things that is true, but
yet people don't ever talk about out
loud, and I don't understand why. So, I
want to share it here. So, let's start
here. Have you ever watched interviews
with professionals in the sports world,
like pro basketball players, football

And have you ever watched one of the

Now, many of them will admit how poorly

one-on-one against me. Now, I haven't

playing terribly from the NBA, he would

Because compared to other professionals,
yes, he played terribly, but compared to

it's sold thousands of copies and has

## Why can't I stay consistent with my writing?

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=33yvQVsrTHU>

Primary Topic: Writing Mindset & Productivity
Secondary Topics: Character
Tertiary Topics: Motivation & Desire, Beats, Coaching & Mentorship, Audience, Editing, Feedback

If you've ever started five novels at
once, but then finished zero of them, if
you've ever had a burst of writing
energy where you produced 10,000 words
in a day, and then didn't write again
for 3 months, if you've ever beaten
yourself up for lacking discipline, this
video is for you. And I want to start by
telling you it's not a discipline
problem. About one in five writers that
we talk to at Story Grid mentions ADHD,
autism, or some other form of
neurodivergence. That's a huge number,
and they all describe the same pattern.
One writer put it perfectly. He said,
"My ADHD makes me hyperfocus, which
means I can either procrastinate and
drive you insane, or I can sit down one
day and have 10,000 words written."
Another said, "I am ADHD, so I can get
distracted very easily. The blank page
syndrome happens a lot." And here's how
the cycle works. You get a new story
idea, it's exciting, you dive in, the
dopamine is flowing, you write like
crazy for days or weeks, then the
excitement fades. Something new catches
your attention. The novel you're working
on, it goes on the shelf with all of
those others. Now, if you're nodding
along right now, I want you to hear this
clearly. That is not a character flaw.
That's how your brain works, and it's
not going to change by trying harder.
The issue here isn't motivation or
discipline or willpower. The issue is
that you're trying to write in a system
or without a system that was never
designed for how your brain operates.
Neurodivergent brains need three things
to sustain momentum. External deadlines,
external accountability, and a clear
next step. Without those three things,
the internal motivation eventually
drains, and the project stalls. That is
exactly what an editor mentor provides.
Every week you have a scene due, not
whenever you feel like it. A specific
deadline. Every week a mentor reads it
and gives feedback. Not optional,
someone is expecting your work, and
every week you know exactly what to work
on next. No staring at a blank page
wondering where to start. One writer
told us, "I get overwhelmed, and then I
procrastinate, and then I don't do it.
But I really want to do it."
The wanting was never the problem. The
structure was. Think of it this way. You
don't need more motivation. You need a
system that doesn't depend on motivation
to keep it going. Because motivation is
unreliable for everyone, and especially
for you. So, if you've been calling
yourself undisciplined, if you've been
beating yourself up for not having
enough motivation, I really want you to
stop. You've got the creativity, you've
got the ideas, you've got the talent.
What you need is a structure in place
that funnels that creativity, that gives
you the accountability to make sure you
actually make real progress, and works
with your brain instead of against it.

## Won't my structure make my writing feel generic?

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9rUvMSKg43M>
Caption file: 9rUvMSKg43M.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Story Structure
Secondary Topics: Reader Experience & Engagement
Tertiary Topics: Audience, Motivation & Desire, Beta Readers

Nobody thinks that J.R.R. Tolkien and
Jane Austen wrote the same book. One
wrote about hobbits and dark lords, the
other wrote about marriage and manners
in English country houses. Completely
different worlds, completely different
stories, but they both use the same
structural principles, and so does every
other novel you've ever loved. A lot of
writers resist the idea of structure
because they think it means formula.
They think it means their quiet literary
novel is going to come out sounding like
a Marvel movie. In fact, one writer told
us that she felt that structure books
were breaking it down to really boring
sort of things that I don't want to
write. She also said, "I don't write
exciting stories." And she thought that
meant structure didn't apply to her. But
here's the thing. Her soggy middles were
caused by a lack of structure. The
reason the middle felt boring to her and
her beta readers wasn't because her
story was too quiet, it was because the
scenes didn't have enough at stake to
pull the reader forward and keep them
turning pages. Structure isn't a
formula. It's the invisible skeleton
that makes every unique story work. It's
the reason you keep turning pages
without knowing why. It's the reason you
cry at the ending even though you saw it
coming.
You could write about ants marching on a
sidewalk, and if the structure is there,
people will care and read every word.
Structure doesn't limit creativity, it
channels it. It gives your reader the
experience they came for, the feeling
that the story works, that it's going
somewhere, that it means something. Your
story isn't too complex for structure,
your story is complex because it needs
structure to hold it together. And no
matter how much you maybe have even
studied structure, you have not been
taught the skills to actually put it in
your writing and make the writing work.
And so, if you've been resisting
structure because you thought it would
make your writing generic, the opposite
is true. Structure is what allows your
unique voice to land on the page and
keep the readers turning pages, crying
at the end, and then handing it to a
friend so they'll read it, too.

Secondary Topics: None

The other day, a writer told me that her
husband sees her writing as a hobby. In
fact, he told her to just stick with her
day job, retire, get her pension, and
then maybe she could focus on her
writing at that point. But then what she
told me is that writing is her passion.
That when she's writing, she's filled
with joy and creativity and energy, and
she thinks this is what she's actually
meant to do. So, which one of them is
right? A lot of writers have
internalized the message that writing
isn't a real pursuit. It comes from
spouses, parents, friends, society.
Another writer said that his wife told
him he should just stop because it's
never going to be profitable.
And over time, that message gets inside
your head. You start apologizing for
wanting to write. You feel guilty about
spending time on it. You definitely feel
guilty about spending money on it. But
here's what I've noticed. The people who
treat writing like a hobby get hobby
results. And then they point to those
results and say, "See, it was just a
hobby." It's a self-fulfilling prophecy.
But here's what I want you to think
about with your life. How many things do
you spend money on that don't have a
monetary value at the end? Most of the
things that you spend money on are
things that make your life better.
Vacations that improve your life,
learning other skills, working out. All
of these things that don't add money to
your life, but they make you a better
human. They get you closer to the things
that you're passionate about. They help
you actually improve in the ways that
you care about and will matter at the
end of your life.
Writing fiction is a skill, a real,
trainable, measurable skill.
But here's the thing. You shouldn't
pursue it just so that you can get rich
and publish a big bestseller.
You should pursue it because it's worth
pursuing. That in that pursuit, you will
become the human you've always wanted to
be. You will finally accomplish that
thing that you've wanted to do since you
were 9 years old and didn't care about
money at all.
Doing this means something to the world.
The only way to make the world a better
place is to tell better stories, and our
world needs your story. And I want you
to get it out before you die. I want you
to publish something you're proud of
that makes you proud to give it to your
friends and family and leaves a legacy
long after you're gone. You don't have
to quit your day job tomorrow. That's
not the goal here. is to take this thing
that you care about and take it
seriously. If writing is a thing that
fills you with joy and energy and
purpose, and you know this is who you
are. If you think about your story every
day, even when you're not writing, this

One of the writers I spoke with is 58

years, and she told me, "It's now or

Another writer, he retired 2 years ago
convinced he'd finally write his novel.
2 years later, he's still on chapter
one. So, when is the right time? I talk
to writers day in and day out who tell
me the timing isn't right. And for many
of them, maybe it isn't. They're dealing
with health issues or caring for a sick
parent, or they just lost a loved one.
Life is hard. I completely get it.
And here's what I've also noticed. The
writers who wait for the perfect time
are still waiting years later because
the perfect time never comes. There's
always a reason not to do this. One
writer has been saying, "Finish it this
year" for 4 years in a row. Same goal, 4
years, nothing has changed. Not because
she's lazy, but because nothing in her
process has actually changed so that
she'll move forward. Now, I'm not going
to pressure you. If now isn't the right
time for some reason, you're a grown
person, you can make your own decisions.
Obviously, I respect that.
But, if you're waiting for some magical
moment in the future when your life is
going to open up and you're going to
have all this time, money, and
resources, and energy to work on your
writing,
will that ever actually come? What I
found for myself and the writers I work
with are that you have to learn to make
it happen in the middle of your messy
life. There's never going to be a
perfect time. There's never going to be
a time where everything is smooth.
Things aren't going to clear up in 3
months. And you have to learn how to
keep writing even when your life is
messy. Because let's say that magical
time does open up for 3 months, and you
get to work on your writing, what
happens when your life starts getting
messy again? Well, you haven't built up
the habit of doing it anyway, you're
going to end up stop writing, and you're
going to get stuck again. So, here's the
thing. If your writing is important to
you, and you've been saying, "I'm going
to do it tomorrow. I'm going to do it
someday" year after year after year, or
you've been kind of working on it but
not making real progress, at some point
you've got to decide, is this important
enough to make it fit in my life and
start making it happen?

Well, because coaching is a completely

design training, and push you past

your scene and say, here's what's not
working and here's why. That's a
completely different skill set than
actually writing a novel. Our editor
mentors go through 6 months of intensive

to diagnose, how to give feedback that

what you're getting when you work with
us. And the proof isn't in the mentors'
bibliography, it's in the student
results. We publish books from our

copies and gotten lots and lots of
reviews. We publish their work in our
own literary magazine, and many, many of
our students have gone out and gotten
their work published in different
literary magazines around the world.

editorial team, not by what they've
written, by what their students, the
writers they've actually worked with,

## Can't I use ChatGPT instead of a writing coach?

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yp8Gyi_egEg>
Caption file: yp8Gyi_egEg.en.vtt
Primary Topic: AI & Writing Tools
Secondary Topics: Writer Development
Tertiary Topics: AI / ChatGPT, Coaching & Mentorship, Audience, Feedback, Motivation & Desire, Antagonist, Conflict & Stakes, Dialogue

I spoke to a writer recently who told me
that she's using chat GPT as a writing
coach. She said, "I tell it do not write
the scene for me, but how would I go
about doing this?" Then she paused and
said,
"But it's not quite the same as a real
person." And she's right, and I want to
tell you why. Let me be fair.
AI can be a useful tool. It can
brainstorm with you. It can maybe
explain some concepts. It can help be a
really good thesaurus so you can find
that perfect word. So, those are real
uses and I'm not going to pretend that
they're not. But here's what AI cannot
do. It can't read your scene in the
context of your genre, your character
arc, your story promise, and your
specific skill level and give you a
diagnosis that actually makes you a
better writer. AI doesn't know that your
inciting incident isn't landing because
the value shift isn't clear enough for a
book in the thriller genre. It doesn't
know that your dialogue feels stilted
because you're using it as exposition.
It doesn't know that your middle is
sagging because the antagonist pressure
isn't escalating. What AI gives you is
generic advice that sounds good. Try
adding some more sensory detail. Show,
don't tell. Make the stakes higher. But
you already know that. It's the same
advice craft books give you all the
time, and we've already established that
more generic advice isn't what's
actually going to break through for you.
You'll also notice the more that you try
to work with AI on your writing is that
it will give you kind of random and
contradictory advice. So, you'll ask it
the same question three different times
over three different days and you'll get
three different answers, which means you
can't rely on its feedback and what it's
actually telling you.
The other thing AI can't do is hold you
accountable. It doesn't care if you skip
a week. It doesn't push you when you're
avoiding the hard scene. It doesn't
notice that you've been stuck on the
same problem for 3 months. An editor
mentor does. AI is a tool, like a word
processor or a thesaurus. It's useful,
but a tool isn't a teacher or a coach.
And what you need right now isn't a
tool, it's a trained human being who can
see what you can't see in your writing
and push you to make those changes that
are blind spots for you. So, sure, use
chat GPT for brainstorming, use it for
research. It's a great thesaurus. But
don't think that it's a substitute for
real craft feedback. That is not what
it's built for and it can't do it.

described this cycle to me perfectly. He

it? You probably know more about story

So, why are you still stuck? Here's what
I've noticed after hundreds of
conversations with writers. Almost every
single one of them can define the
elements of a great story, the inciting
incident, crisis, climax, character
development, all that stuff. They can
name them. They can spot them in their
favorite novels. But, when they sit down
to write their own scene, it falls flat
and they can't figure out why. One
writer told us straight up, "I
understand the five commandments, but I
don't always know how to apply them."
Another said she would read a well-known
structure book with her writing partner
and still couldn't make heads or tails
of it when she sat down to write. And
this isn't because you're not smart

concept and executing that concept in
your writing are two completely
different skills. They live in different
parts of your brain. So, think about
learning the piano. You could study
music theory for years. You could
understand chord progressions, time
signatures, key changes, all of it
intellectually. But, the first time you
sit down at a piano, your fingers don't
know any of that. You need someone
sitting next to you saying, "No, your
hand position is off. Try it this way.
Do you hear the difference?" That's how
the theory becomes muscle memory.

theory only becomes skill when someone
watches you apply it and corrects you in
real time. This is why at Story Grid, we
don't start by teaching you more theory.

we do is give you a scene to write, a
specific, focused exercise designed to
isolate just one skill at a time. Then,
an editor mentor reads it. Not to grade
you, not to say nice job, but to say,
"Here's where the inciting incident
isn't landing and here's specifically is
why and here's what to try instead." You
rewrite it, they read it again, and
suddenly, the concept you understood
intellectually for years clicks in your
actual writing for the first time.

application. And it's the reason writers
who've been studying craft for a decade
can level up in months once they have
the right feedback. So, if you've been
reading craft books and taking courses

clicking, it's not you. It's just that
nobody's shown you how to take what you
know and actually put it on the page.

## The Hidden Power of Verbs (No One Teaches You This)

Let's get right into it. Take the verb
walked for instance. There are so many
options for portraying to the reader
that the character walked. You could use
stomped, marched, stroed, stalked,
stormed, charged, advanced, thundered,
crept, tiptoed, slinkedked, and so many
more that you see on your screen right
now. So, how do you choose which verb to
use? You may think it's obvious, or
you'll know it when you're writing.
it'll just come to you or maybe even the
muse will tell you. But we review
hundreds of scenes from writers every
month and I'll tell you it's not that
simple. So, let's walk through it
together. There are three questions to
ensure that you pick the perfect verb
every time. Number one, who are you
telling the story to? Who is your single
audience member? If you're telling the
story to a friend at a bar, you might
use the phrase, "She her pants."
But if you're telling the story to your
Sunday school teacher, you're probably
going to go with something else. Number
two, why are you telling the story? You,
the writer, should have an opinion about
what is going on. You can portray to the
reader what you want them to think about
what is happening by the verbs you
choose. If you say a man slithered
across the street versus he dragged
across the street, you give different
information to the reader even though
the end result of the action is the same
in both cases. The man walked across the
street. Number three, what do you want
the reader to feel about what is going
on? Do you want them to feel creeped
out? Then you might use slithered. Do
you want them to feel sympathetic? You
might use limped. Do you want them to
feel anger? You might use stumped.
Amused, you might use sacheted. Anxious,
raced. Calm, doawled. So you see, simply
by choosing a different type verb,
you're going to portray a different
emotion that you want the reader to
feel. So again, the three questions to
pick the perfect verb every time are
one, who are you telling the story to?
Number two, why are you telling them the
story? And number three, what do you
want the reader to feel about what is
going on? Now, there are two rules that
you must follow when you are choosing
these verbs. Number one, don't be
neutral. The reader is relying on you to
indicate to them how they should feel
about what is going on in the story. If
you pick nothing but neutral verbs, they
will feel lost and confused, which means
they will stop reading and move on to a
better writer. So number one is don't be
neutral. Number two is be consistent. If
you want the reader to feel anxious,
pick anxious verbs. Angry then angry
verbs. Amused then amused verbs. The
only thing worse than being neutral is
being inconsistent because the reader
will feel yanked around emotionally and
not know what to think, which again
means they will close the book and move
on to a better writer. So, the two rules
in picking your verbs are don't be
neutral and be consistent. Have one
emotion you're trying to evoke in the
reader and stick to that over and over
and over. If you do this, you'll start
writing page turning fiction that
readers will love. But here's the thing,
picking the right verb is just one of
the many skills you have to get right in
order to write page turning fiction that

that emotion wash over you. For me,
several years ago, I felt terror when I

one of them broke free of my hand and
started running towards the busy road.

when I thought my marriage was over and
I was about to lose everything. So step
two is to identify a time in your life
when you have had that exact same
intense emotion you want the reader to
feel. Go back to that time in your life.
Think about what it was like, what you
felt like, and what was going on. Which
then leads to step three. Now write the
scene so your readers feel exactly what
you felt. Everything you choose to
write, the action, dialogue, setting,
description, exposition, should be
chosen to make your reader feel that one
emotion. Choose the verbs, nouns, and
descriptors, adverbs, and adjectives

inciting incident. The inciting incident

be something unavoidable that the

incident come from? The source is
antagonism.

thing, the inciting incident can be bad,

your job or a bomb threat or a breakup.
But an inciting incident can also be a
good thing, like meeting the love of
your life or getting offered a job. It's
like this. The protagonist is going
along in their life thinking they know
what's going to happen next, just doing
their thing. then antagonism gets in the
way and forces them to do something
different. So the inciting incident is a

of chaos into your protagonist
wellplanned life. And the antagonist
wants something too. They want the
protagonist to do something they don't
want to do. We're going to play this out
in three different scenarios. The first,
a guy loses his job. That's the inciting
incident. The second, a woman meets a
man of her dreams, only it's not the man
that is currently her boyfriend. And
third, a woman is hiking through the

So, what happens when you get fired?
Well, you want to keep your job without
having to sacrifice your dignity. What

them without letting go of the current
relationship. And when you come across a
tiger that wants to eat you in the
jungle, you want to get away without
being eaten. Number four, progressive
complications and turning point. Because
of the inciting incident, your
protagonist now has a problem. They have
to deal with this force of antagonism
and they start trying to do different
things so that they don't actually have
to deal with the source of antagonism.

going to do what the antagonist wants."
So he says, "I'm not leaving the office.
I'm not accepting being fired." So to
this man that she's met, she offers to
just stay friends so she can keep both
relationships in her life. And for the
person running from the tiger, she
reaches the edge of a cliff and turns
back because she doesn't want to jump.
She's not going to keep running. Now the
natural result of this turning point is
number three, the crisis. It's the
ultimatum. It comes from the antagonist
and it forces a choice between A or B. A
choice between two decisions that have
irreversibility into it. Meaning both of
the decisions have really high
consequences. Because up until this
point, your protagonist is trying to
have their cake and eat it too. They
want to get what they want without

there has to be downsides on both sides
because if we put our protagonist in
between drinking poison and eating a
piece of cake, well, that's kind of

interesting. They're choosing between

consequences. And here's the thing, the

alongside them. So why does this work?
Well, it's because we recognize

just go deep here and look at one

Games. So, she responds to chaos. So,
she's living in her normal world and
then her sister gets pulled into the
Hunger Games and she's got to step up

at the beginning. That's the inciting
incident of the entire story. And she
steps up and takes her place. And what
that means is she's a fish out of water.
She's got to leave her hometown and go
into the Hunger Games. And then she has
a clear object of desire. She wants to

to get to work on time. They want their
boyfriend to tell them that they love

thinking through my character's object
of desire is they have to want X without
having to Y. They have to want
something, but there's this constraint.

mentor. Or Jon wants to tell the truth

enemies. Now there's conflict baked into

objects of desire that they are

## Pantser vs Plotter: The Right Way to Write

Primary Topic: Story Structure
Secondary Topics: Writer Development, Writing Craft

There's this dichotomy in writing
between the pantsers and the plotters.
And on one side, the pantsers say,
"Well, you just follow the muse, you
take your idea for a book, and you just
start writing. And through the process
of writing, you find what your book is.
You just need the setup or the
characters or some good idea for your
story, and then you just start writing."
And then on the other side are the
plotters. And the plotters are the
people that want to plan out their story
before they actually write it. And so
they start thinking through all the
different plot elements and the
characters and how they're going to arc
and all this kind of stuff. And the
problem with that is both of them
produce bad writing. In my early days of
writing, I was a big plotter. I was the
one that wanted to figure out everything
before I wrote anything. I thought this
would save me from writing a bad book.
And really what it did is it just set me
up to write a bad book. But then I've
also seen the pantser side of the
equation, and that doesn't actually
produce a great book, either.

would get lost in the forest, run out of
food, get eaten by a bear, run out of
water, and never find their way out. And
so, when my friend was taught how to do
orienteering, he wasn't taught to figure
it out intuitively. He was taught it
explicitly. So, he had a teacher that
took him out into the woods and taught
him all of the different skills that go
into surviving in a forest. How to use a
compass, how to read the sun, how to
read rivers and trees and all of these
things that I don't know how to do, but
somebody taught him how to do those, and
he learned them so well that over time
he was able to move them from explicit
understanding
to intuitive understanding. And this is
how we learn almost anything. You think
about when you first learn how to ride a
bike, you're focusing really hard on the
handlebars and how to steer them or how
to pedal or how to balance. And then you
had somebody that was teaching you how
to do all of these things explicitly.
And then as you learn them, they became
intuitive. Where now you can probably
ride a bike while not even thinking
about it. So here's the point I want to
make about pantser verse plotter. So
we're going to have this guy and we're
going to say that he's the pantser. And
then we're going to have this girl and
we're going to say that she's the
plotter. So the pantser is going to have
a basic idea for a story and then enter
the woods and then generally
hit all of these marks and then come out
the other end with a story.
The plotter is going to plan ahead
thinking through all of these things.
But they're also going to hit all the
same marks
and come out with a working story. The
difference between what's happening here
is that these
are pros. And what we're dealing with
most of the time when we're arguing
pantser verse plotter is we're dealing
with amateurs. This is what I was when I
was trying to plot out my story and I
would work really hard to plot out my
story then I sit down and wrote it and
then I came out with something that was
not a story. That's because I was an
amateur writer and I didn't understand
how to do all the things that actually
takes to write a story. And so whether
or not you're a pantser or a plotter
does not matter what comes out the other
end. It's whether or not you're pro or
you're an amateur.
And so here's the big point I want to
make. There are skills that go into
writing. These are everything from your
line-by-line writing and how to write a
great sentence to the five commandments
of storytelling to genre and obligatory
moments and conventions. There's all
these different skills that go into it.
I'm just going to keep writing down
plot, character development, action, and
exposition. But again, these are just a
handful. There's a lot of them. So,
these are all the skills. So, no matter
whether you are a pantser or you are a
plotter, you have to learn the same
skills. The same things show up in
working stories. So, here's my question
to you.
How do you want to learn these?
Do you want to be
like the amateur pantsers, which is how
Stephen King started, who goes into the
woods and for years and years
they wander around, wander around,
wander around, eventually pick up all of
these skills, and start learning how to
come out the other end with a book? Or
would you want to learn these skills the
same way my buddy learned orienteering,
where somebody walked them through
learning the skills, and it was a lot
easier to learn the skills and start
coming out the other side? So, this is
my point when people talk about how
"Well, I have to write a 200,000 words
of my novel before I can actually figure
out what I'm trying to say." And I'm
like, "Okay, that works the same way,
you know, if I live in Los Angeles and I
want to get to New York City, uh I can
walk to get there. I will eventually
find myself there,
but there are more efficient ways to
actually do things. So, when you're
trying to pick up all of these skills of
writing that you have to learn, again,
from the sentence up to the scene, up to
the full story,
you can write and write and write and
write and write for years and years and
years and hope that you eventually find
them, or you can figure out what those
skills are and learn them on purpose.
So, here's the big thing I want you to
take away, and it took me a long time to
really face this within myself. That the
dichotomy is not between pantser and
plotter. That doesn't actually matter.
That's much more of a preference than
whether or not it actually matters. The
real thing that matters are do you have
the skills in order to write a great
story? Because these are skills that you
can learn, just like you can learn any
other skills, is how to write a great
story. And the real choice is not
between pantser and plotter. The real
choice is are you going to randomly just
keep writing words for a really long
time hoping eventually you'll learn
these skills, or are you going to slow
down, just like my friend did when he
wanted to learn orienteering? just grab
a compass and run off into the woods. He
found somebody that could actually walk
him through developing the skills. And I
know for myself, I tried for years and
years and years to write by just writing
words and writing words and writing
words, and then I found Shawn Coyne, the
creator and founder of Story Grid, and
he actually started systematically
walking me through how to pick up these
skills, and that's when I actually
became the writer that I wanted to be.
Now, if you're wondering what these
skills are, I've got something great for
you, because here at Story Grid, the
thing that we focus on first is how to
write a really great scene. If you can
write one great scene that gets somebody
to read to the end and be excited to
keep reading, now you're on the right
track. And we have our 13-point scene
writing checklist that we use here at
Story Grid to both teach scene writing
and evaluate how somebody did. And I
want to give that to you right now. So,
if you go to storygrid.com/checklist,
you can download the exact 13-point
scene writing checklist that we use here
at Story Grid to both write our scenes
and evaluate where writers are at with
these skills. If I could go back in time
and start over with my writing journey,
the one big change I would make is
realize it's not just about churning out
words, it's not just about finishing a
novel, it's not just about telling the
story that's in my heart. It's about
systematically learning the skills of
how to write something great. And then,
then I will have the skills to take that
story that's inside of myself and get it
out to the world. Our goal here at Story
Grid is to help you build the skills,
write a book, and leave your legacy.
That's why we put out so many free
videos here on YouTube. That's why
there's so many resources on our website
is we want to help you do this. If you
want to dig deeper into this, I highly
recommend you join us for our next
workshop. It's starting next month. It's

to actually apply these skills and level
up your writing. So, go to
storygrid.com/workshop
to check that out as well. The links to
both the workshop and the checklist are
down in the description. Also, if you
like this video, if anything in this was

I'm going to put that up on the screen

A few years ago, I really hit a wall
with my scene writing. I was having
trouble figuring out how to write
different scenes from different
perspectives that might be in different
types of books. And I was just getting
stuck over and over trying to figure out
how I could consistently write great
scenes. And so Shawn Coin and I were
working together on this. And Shawn is
the creator and founder of Story Grid.
He's the guy with over 30 years
experience as a writer, editor, and
story researcher. and everything a story
grid is based on his writing and
research. And so we were working
together on this problem and I kept just
running into this wall and he was having
trouble getting me to understand all
these different things I needed to wrap
my head around if I was actually going
to level up my scene writing until we
hit a breakthrough. He had me write this
scene and then I iterated on a few
drafts until he said it was working
really well. And then we were talking
about it and he said, "You know, you
told this story, you wrote this scene as
if it was a guy telling his friends at
the bar what happened." So, you wrote
this scene, it's really crass and you're
kind of the hero of it and it's kind of
funny. It comes across like you're
telling the story to your friends at the
bar. So, he had me rewrite the scene
again. Now, the original was in first
person. And he said, "Keep it first
person." But instead of writing it as if
you're telling your friends at the bar,
"Tell the same story, but as if you're
telling it to your 8-year-old daughter,
and you're trying to get her to be mad
at your ex-wife, which is her mom." So,
it's a different moral to the story, and
you're telling a completely different
person. So, I went to do that and all of
a sudden, I started realizing, well,
this changes everything. It changes what
I'm going to point out in the scene. Uh
who I'm going to talk about in the
scene, why I'm telling the story. It's
going to change the kind of language I'm
using if I'm telling my friends at a bar
verse telling my 8-year-old daughter.
So, I did that again. Wrote a couple
drafts until he was happy with it. And
now he's like, "Okay, rewrite the scene
again, but this time he's telling his
priest and he's trying to get his priest
to give him absolution." So, again, this
changes everything. It changes the words
I use and how I explain it and the moral
of the story and all of these different
things. So, I'm telling the same exact
event, the same scene, but all of a
sudden everything changes if it changes
who I'm telling it to and the reason I'm
telling it to them. Now, what we're
talking about here is the narrative
device. And the narrative device is made
up of three parts. The first is the
author. Now, the author isn't you like
the full instantiation of who you are.
The author is a role that you're
playing. And we do this all the time.
When I'm interacting with my
eight-year-old daughter, I'm playing the
role of father. When I'm interacting
with my friends at a bar, I'm playing
the role of friend. When I'm interacting
with a priest, I'm interacting as a
parishioner. Right? So, we automatically
play different roles in our life. And
those are never the full instantiation
of who we are, but they're a part that
we play. And so the author when you're
writing your story is a part that you're
playing when you're writing the story.
It's the role that you're filling in
your story. So that's the first part of
the narrative device. The second part is
the single audience member. And we refer
to this person as Sam. So whenever I use
the word Sam, this is who I'm talking
about. And this is the person you're
telling the story to. So we say at Story
Grid all the time that specificity
breeds universality. So the more
specific you make your story, the more
universal it becomes. And the way that
we do this at Story Grid is we write our
story to one person, the single audience
member. And we have that person firmly
in our mind when we're telling our
story. And then the last piece of the
narrative device is the problem. Why are
we telling the story? Why are we telling
the story to Sam? And why is Sam
listening to the story? This is the
problem. So the narrative devices made
up of the author, the Sam, and the
problem. And what you see as you mess
around with these things is it
completely changes everything in your
story. So let's go through an example
here. So I'm going to give you a story
setup. When I was 17 years old, I got
blackout drunk at a party and woke up in
an emerald green banquet dress in high
heels in a dumpster behind a Walmart.
Now, this never actually happened, or at
least that's the story I'm going to
tell. But imagine we're going to tell
this story and we're going to tell it
using this narrative device. The author
is now a father, right? So instead of
him being 17 years old, this is in the
future and he's playing the role of a
father when he's telling the story. And
he's telling this story to his
17-year-old son. And the problem they're
both facing is that the son wants to go
to a party with alcohol and the father
wants him to not go. And here's the
reason why he doesn't want him to go.
That's why he's telling him this story.
So, what kind of language is the father
going to use? What's the moral of the
story going to be? And how is he going
to come at telling this story to his
17-year-old son when he's trying to warn

young age? Okay. So, we're going to tell
the same story, the same exact story,
but we're going to change up that
narrative device. Now, you're a
43year-old guy. You're Sam. Your single
audience member is a high school buddy.
Y'all are at a bar and you're trying to
reconnect over shared memories. So, you
start telling this story, retelling the
story probably about when you were 17
years old and got drunk and ended up in
a dress behind a Walmart. Well, again,
what kind of language are you going to
use? What's the moral of the story?
There's probably a lot more laughter.
You're probably going to play down the
really embarrassing parts and play up
the really funny parts. And it's going
to completely change how you present
this story to Sam. Again, exact same
story. And now we're going to change it
again. And we're going to do it similar
to an example I used a minute ago.
You're a 17-year-old. So this happened
to you this past weekend. You're telling
the story to a priest. And you're trying
to get absolution. So again, the kind of
language you're going to use, how you're
going to set it up, the moral of the
story, which parts are you going to play

everything? You see really quickly this
completely changes everything in your
story. What you're describing, the
things that you're pointing out in the
story, the things you leave out of the
story. Again, the type of language
you're using, how balanced the language
is, all of these things play into how
you're going to tell your story. Okay,
here's the exercise. Here's what I want
you to do. I want you to take a scene
that you've written recently. And if you
haven't written one, just go write one.
And I want you to start playing with
these things. Rewrite the exact same
scene. Tell the exact same story, but
you're going to do it by changing up the
author. And then you're going to change
up the Sam. And then you're going to
change up the problem. And you're going
to do this several different times. And
this goes for point of view, too. You
can change up if you're telling it in
first person or third person. Imagine
I'm that father again telling the story
to my son, but I'm telling it about some
other 17-year-old that woke up behind
the Walmart in a dumpster, right? So, I
can still tell it in third person. You
can also change up how you're telling

do this, just take one scene and write

six, seven times, by changing up all of
these different things, you're going to
learn. so much, right? So many times I
get questions about, well, how do you
put description in? How do you put

## The Scene Planning Framework Every Writer Needs

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M15bb6DQiPA>
Caption file: M15bb6DQiPA.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Scene Craft
Secondary Topics: Character, Story Structure
Tertiary Topics: Motivation & Desire, Protagonist, Inciting Incident, Conflict & Stakes, Crisis, Climax, Tension, Turning Point

Julie is an inspiring writer and she
sent me a scene from her work in
progress that she had just written and
she wanted me to analyze and give her
feedback to see what was right what was
wrong and how she could make it better
so I took the scene I read it and at the
end I thought holy this is so bad I
don't think I could do anything to help
this person with their writing this was
one of the worst things I had ever read
There were random characters that were
in there for no good reason I couldn't
really tell what the scene was about
where it was going there was no Arc to
it no story to it and this was something
that she wanted to put in her book and
actually be part of the book and I had
no idea how to help her and my problem
she had paid me to help her become a
better writer and actually level up her
scene writing and I didn't want to give
her the money back so I had to figure
out how to actually help her so I said
hey Julie let's get on a call we got on
a call I said okay grab a piece of paper
and we're going to write down three
things the first thing I had Julie write
down is who is the protagonist who is
this scene about who do we want the
reader to empathize with in this scene
and who is the protagonist that we're
going to track and see actually make the
climatic decision so who is the
protagonist of the scene that was the
first thing I had Julie write down the
second thing I had Julie write down is
the inciting incident now the inciting
incident is the thing that comes along
and knocks your protagonist life off of
balance now this doesn't mean that your
protagonist life was going perfectly at
the beginning of the scene it just means
they thought they knew what would happen
next this is how all of us go through
our life we get up in the morning and we
have a plan for the day and then
something comes along and messes up that
plan and this doesn't have to be a bad
thing an inciting incident could be a
good thing it could be a job offer it
could be meeting somebody the
protagonist is going to fall in love
with but often it's a bad thing and it
could be a big thing like a threat in an
action story or a cancer diagnosis but
it can be a small thing too where you
stumble out at 5:30 in the morning and
you open up the container where there's
coffee grounds and there's no coffee
grounds because your spouse got up
before you and drank the last cup of
coffee that could be an insiding
incident whatever it is what did your
protagonists think was their plans for
the day and what came came in and
screwed all that up what was the
inciting incident of your scene that's
the second thing the third thing I had
Julie write down is what is the object
of Desire that came as a result of the
inciting incident so your protagonist
life got knocked off balance because of
the inciting incident and that has to
bring up a desire there has to be
something that they want this is where
the tension and conflict in the scene
comes from is their object of Desire so
I told Julie on her piece of paper to
write down the object of desire and to
do it in this formula my protagonist
wants X without having to Y so your
protagonist has to want something but
there has to be something they're not
wanting to give up in order to get that
thing so it could be I want coffee
without having to leave the house I want
my boyfriend to tell me he loves me
without me having to say it first I want
to get the new job without having to
move to Manhattan so you have to have a
situation where your protagonist can't
have their cake and eat it too this is
what we all want we want to get what we
want but we don't want to have to give
up something to get it and we want to
put your protagonist in that particular
spot as well is they have something that
they want that comes out out of the
inciting incident but they have to have
this thing that they don't want to give
up or don't have to do in order to get
that thing so once Julie had these three
things written down she was ready to
rewrite her scene she knew who the
protagonist was she had the inciting
incident and she had the object of
Desire because just having those three
things gives you so many things about
your scene because here's what you know
already first you know what the turning
point of the scene is going to be
something is going to happen to your
protagonist where they realize they
can't have their cake and eat it too
they're either not going to get what
they want or in order to get what they
want they're going to have to do that
thing they didn't want to do so that's
theer turning point of the scene when
that rubber band snaps and the
protagonist realizes they can't have
their cake and eat it too that's going
to be the turning point of the scene and
then that leads to the crisis and the
crisis is always a question which is is
your protagonist going to do X or are
they going to do why and that is going
to be the crisis that comes out of the
object of Desire are they going to get
what they want but have to give up that
thing or have to do that thing they
didn't want to do or are they just not
going to get what they want
and then that drives us all the way to
the climax and this is where we see your
character actually take action and this
is the most important part of the scene
because this is where we see the true
character of the character so given that
case of me waking up in the morning and
there's no coffee grounds and now I want
coffee without having to leave the house
now you will get to see how important
coffee actually is to me will I just not
have coffee today so I don't get what I
want or will I get in the car and drive
somewhere at 5:30 in the morning to get
a cup of coffee that is the climax when
the protagonist makes the decision and
then the resolution is what happens as a
result of that decision so just making
those three choices gives you a huge
amount of information to write your
scene you got to know who the
protagonist is what the inciting
incident is and what the object of
Desire is so what happened for Julie so
I walked her through this I had her
write all this down I said okay go try
to write your next scene and I just sat
with baited breath and crossed fingers
for a couple days until I got to see her
next scene and when she turned it in it
was so much better there were Stakes
there was tension there was excitement
and the writing compelled me all the way
to the end she had a working scene now
was there more problems to fix of course
was the scene perfect of course not but
it switched from not working to working
because she had clear change in her
story because she knew who the
protagonist was she knew the inciting
incident and she knew the object of
Desire so for you the next time you
write the next scene in your work in
progress I recommend jotting these down
right at the beginning making these
decisions about how the scene is going
to start who the protagonist is the
inciting incident and what the object of
Desire is and make sure the object of
Desire is worded that way the
protagonist wants X without having to Y

I'm trying to write something that I can

to write, and I'm hoping that what I

those two things just don't go together

role of a grandfather and he's telling
the story to his grandchild to answer
the question when do you stay home and
stay safe and when do you risk adventure
and explore the world and if you reread
the Hobbit with that in mind with this
idea of a grandfather telling a story to
his grandchild you'll see it show up
over and over and over you'll see it in
the language that's used how it's simple
and straightforward the way he describes
things and even in a couple moments in
the book where he steps out of the story
and he assures the reader that Bilbo is
going to be okay that's exactly what you
would do to your grandchild when you're
telling them a scary story about goblins
so let's look at another example crazy
Rich Asians by Kevin Quan the author is
Kevin Quan playing the role of an older
wiser woman the Sam is a young naive
woman who's in love and the problem the
author is trying to help Sam with is
when do you conform to culture in family
and when do you stand out as an
individual and again if you read crazy
Rich Asians with this in mind you'll see
that showing up over and over and over
and finally let's look at the Martian by
Andy Weir the author is Andy we playing
the role of a brilliant
astrophysicist this Sam is a young
ambitious boy and the problem is how do
you overcome an insurmountable problem
and that's what we see when we read the
Martian we see Mark Watney stuck in this
insurmountable problem and the way that
he overcomes It Is by systematically
applying scientific solutions to every
little problem he comes across so if you
read it again with this in mind you'll
see that the language the ideas how the
story is told fits within this narrative
device by identifying your narrative
device it fixes so many problems in your
story it helps you understand what
language to use how much exposition to
put in your story what details to
include what details to leave off what
characters need to be in your story and
so many other things and again the good
news is you do this automatically every
day in your life when you're talking to
other people so all you have to do is
learn how to apply that to your writing
as well now I want to be clear here this
doesn't have to be set in reality all
the time you could be a wisened old
Dragon telling a story to to a young
ambitious Dragon like it can be whatever
you want but it has to be specific we
have to know the exact role that you the
author are playing we have to know your
Sam the specific person you're telling
the story to and the problem you're
trying to help Sam solve now this
doesn't always go on the page this isn't
something you actually write in the book
but you have to have it firmly planted
in your mind in order to tell a clear
coherent story that your reader will
love because specificity breeds
universality while the narrative device

those global patterns so this is
functioning at the blue level
so what you can see here is that we have
these three different concepts that
we're going to use to talk about how to
keep readers reading but they're not
separate at all instead they're looking
at that one concept how to keep readers
turning pages how to keep them caring
about your story and we're looking at
them from all three of the storygrid
trinity planes
and what that means is that we're
looking at it in a comprehensive way
so that no matter how you find your way
into concepts no matter what your
natural mode of thinking is you can find
a way into this fundamental concept and
that's how to keep your readers coming
back again and again to your story

## Part 14 - The Four Core Framework - Morality Story

Source: <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QO5TCTpRIDM>
Caption file: QO5TCTpRIDM.en.vtt
Primary Topic: Story Grid Methodology
Secondary Topics: Genre, Reader Experience & Engagement, Character, Publishing
Tertiary Topics: Four Core Framework, Motivation & Desire, Agents & Querying, Protagonist, Climax, Action Genre, Conflict & Stakes, Crisis

Chapter 14: Morality Story. Human need:
Self-transcendence.
Core life value: Selfishness versus
altruism. Core emotion: Satisfaction or
contempt. Core event: The big choice.
Morality story answers the complex
question, when given a chance to behave
selfishly or altruistically, which will
we choose?
Will we apply our unique gifts of
knowledge, ability, and strength of will
in service of darkness or light?
Morality stories are about making a
choice to act on behalf of ourselves or
others and the consequences of that
choice.
This choice is the culmination of a
protagonist journey from the bottom to
the top of the hierarchy of human needs
that began with action story.
How do you deliver the experience
morality story readers are looking for?
The core need of self-transcendence
arises after the inciting incident
presents a shock to the hibernating self
of the protagonist who has discovered
and expressed their gifts in order to
survive and thrive in the world.
This is the moment when an opportunity
itself for the luminary agent to
contribute to the greater good and leave
something of value in the world after
their death.
The core life value spectrum derived
from the need for self-transcendence
ranges from selfishness to altruism with
several points in between involving
sacrifice for the good of an individual,
the family or tribe, or all of humanity.
When the luminary agent moves beyond
selfish pursuits to express their gifts
for the benefit of others,
readers feel the core emotion of
satisfaction. Perhaps because we feel
inspired to express our gifts for
others, too.
If the luminary withholds altruism and
embraces selfishness, readers may feel
contempt because the world and the
protagonist have both lost an
opportunity to experience transcendence.
Morality story includes three subgenres:
Punitive, redemptive, and testing.
The punitive story follows a protagonist
who is also a villain. They take a
purely selfish path and are punished.
As in the iconic Walter White in the
Breaking Bad TV series or the title
character in Henrik Ibsen's Hedda
Gabler.
The redemption story follows a character
who is lost on the wrong path at the
beginning but recognizes they have
thrown away a great gift and reclaims
that gift to redeem themselves and
achieve altruism by the end as in
Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Scarlet
Letter.
In a testing story with a triumphant
outcome, the protagonist struggles on a
variety of paths wavering before finding
the right one that allows them to
surrender to their purpose.
The film Forrest Gump and the novel For
Whom the Bell Tolls by Ernest Hemingway
are examples of the testing subgenre.
Sometimes characters are tested but can
never escape the selfish path
surrendering to struggle and weakness as
in F. Scott Fitzgerald's Tender Is the
Night.
The universal takeaway or controlling
idea of a morality story that is
positive or prescriptive is we transcend
our own selfishness when we share our
gifts for the benefit of others.
The takeaway when the story ends
negatively or as a cautionary tale is
we are damned when we selfishly withhold
our gifts or use them solely for our own
gain in the world.
If we do succeed in transcending
ourselves to leave a legacy of time well
spent on Earth,
we will add the good we've created to
the collective unconsciousness of Homo
sapiens.
Morality stories demonstrate that our
actions define our character. It's
important to note that morality stories
are not about specific religious or
philosophical systems of belief.
They are about the search for meaning
and purpose that allows us to contribute
to the greater good.
The luminary will have a revelation that
lets them say, "I'm supposed to be doing
this. I can move on and do my work in
the way only I can do it."
This is the sweet spot of being human.
It is the moment when a writer or
painter creates a timeless work of art
that has its own magic to transcend,
inspiring people in the present and
future.
The global crisis of the morality genre
brings us to an extreme point on the
selfishness-altruism spectrum as the
luminary agent faces a dilemma about
whether to express or withhold their
gift in the core event, the big choice
scene. The threat exists that the
luminary will demonstrate selfish
behavior.
The big choice scene, which is both the
global climax and the climax of the
ending payoff, integrates all three core
essentials. The luminary agent's core
need for self-transcendence defines the
core life value of altruism at stake,
which when attained produces a core
emotion response of satisfaction in the
reader.
While the luminary may make any number
of selfish or altruistic choices
throughout the story, it comes down to
the single moment that will make all the
difference. Their selfish or altruistic
choice will determine the outcome for
others, not just themselves.
Summing up,
in morality story, our need for
self-transcendence allows us to identify
with the luminary agent, and we respond
to conflict on the selfishness-altruism
spectrum with satisfaction or contempt
depending on the choice the luminary
makes.
In the core event, the big choice scene,
transcendence is most in jeopardy. The
life value reaches an extreme, and the
core emotion reaches its height.
By setting up and delivering this scene
in an innovative way,
you meet the morality reader's
expectations.
